pages.title: HTTP/1.1 Explained: RFC 9110 and RFC 9112 Messages, Methods and Security | Safeguard Blog
passages: HTTP/1.1 is the text based version of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol: a client sends a request line, header fields and an optional body over a TCP connection, and the server answers with a status line, header fields and a body.
Since June 2022 it has been defined by RFC 9112 (the HTTP/1.1 message syntax), RFC 9110 (the semantics every HTTP version shares) and RFC 9111 (caching), which together replaced RFC 7230 to RFC 7235.
The protocol is old, simple and still everywhere.
## Key takeaways

* HTTP/1.1 is now specified across three documents published in June 2022: RFC 9110 "HTTP Semantics" (STD 97), RFC 9111 "HTTP Caching" (STD 98) and RFC 9112 "HTTP/1.1" (STD 99). RFC 9110 obsoletes RFC 2818 and RFC 7230 to 7235 (except 7234), RFC 9111 obsoletes RFC 7234, and RFC 9112 obsoletes the message syntax parts of RFC 7230.

* A message is a start line, zero or more field lines, an empty line and an optional body. The default port is TCP 80 for `http` URIs and TCP 443 for `https` URIs, per RFC 9110 sections 4.2.1 and 4.2.2.
| RFC 9111 | HTTP Caching | 98 | June 2022 | RFC 7234 |
| RFC 9112 | HTTP/1.1 | 99 | June 2022 | Portions of RFC 7230 |
| RFC 9113 | HTTP/2 | n/a | June 2022 | (HTTP/2 framing, referenced by RFC 9110) |
| RFC 9114 | HTTP/3 | n/a | June 2022 | (HTTP/3 over QUIC, referenced by RFC 9110) |

RFC 9110 now holds everything that applies to every HTTP version: methods, status codes, header field semantics, content negotiation, conditional requests, range requests, authentication, and the `http` and `https` schemes.
| absolute-form | `http://www.example.org/where?q=now` | Requests to a forward proxy |
| authority-form | `www.example.org:443` | CONNECT only, to open a tunnel |
| asterisk-form | `*` | Server wide OPTIONS |
1. A response to HEAD, and any 1xx, 204 or 304 response, ends at the empty line. No body, no matter what the fields say.
2. A 2xx response to CONNECT turns the connection into a tunnel right after the header section.

3. If both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length are present, Transfer-Encoding wins. The RFC adds that such a message "might indicate an attempt to perform request smuggling" and "ought to be handled as an error". An intermediary that forwards it must strip Content-Length first.
| PUT | Replace all current representations with the request content | no | yes |
| DELETE | Remove all current representations | no | yes |
| CONNECT | Establish a tunnel to the server named by the target | no | no |
| RFC 7230 to RFC 7235 | June 2014 | HTTP/1.1 split into six documents (message syntax, semantics, conditional requests, range requests, caching, authentication) |
| RFC 9110, 9111, 9112 | June 2022 | Version independent semantics separated from HTTP/1.1 syntax; stricter parsing to resist smuggling |
| HTTP/2, RFC 9113 | June 2022 | A multiplexed session layer with field compression over TLS and TCP, sharing RFC 9110 semantics |
RFC 9110 says HTTP/1.1 "was introduced in 1995" before its 1997 publication.

RFC 9110 section 17.1 makes the point about plain HTTP directly: for `http` URIs, "any attack on a user's network host table, cached names, or name resolution libraries becomes an avenue for attack on establishing authority".
Section 17.2 adds that intermediaries "are inherently situated for on-path attacks" and are "no more trustworthy than the people and policies under which they operate".
## Weakness classes, explained as concepts
The design allows this because of several historical tolerances:

* **Two length signals.** Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding can both appear. RFC 9112 explains that early implementations sent both, a chunked body plus an estimated length "for use by progress bars", which is why the standard made Transfer-Encoding override Content-Length rather than forbidding the combination. Any hop that does not follow that rule exactly, or that only speaks HTTP/1.0, can disagree with the others.

* **Lenient whitespace and line endings.** RFC 9112 lets recipients treat a bare LF as a line ending and lets them parse request lines on any whitespace. It immediately warns that "lenient parsing can result in request smuggling security vulnerabilities if there are multiple recipients of the message and each has its own unique interpretation of robustness".

* **Field name oddities.** Whitespace before the colon used to be handled differently by different parsers, so RFC 9112 section 5.1 now requires a server to reject it with 400. RFC 9110 section 17.10 describes a related trap in gateway interfaces such as CGI, which map header names to variables by replacing hyphens with underscores; a field named with an underscore could map to the same variable as `Transfer-Encoding`, "resulting in a potential request smuggling vulnerability".

RFC 9112's answer is to make the strict reading mandatory: treat both length fields as an error or strip Content-Length before forwarding, reject invalid or conflicting Content-Length values, reject chunked that is not final in a request, reject whitespace before colons and bare CRs, and close the connection whenever framing was questionable.
RFC 9110 section 17.5 notes that because HTTP uses "mostly textual, character-delimited fields", parsers are often vulnerable to "very long (or very slow) streams of data".

The standard sets minimum sizes that implementations should support but leaves the maximums to operators, and warns that failing to limit method names, field names, numeric values and chunk lengths "can result in arbitrary code execution due to buffer or arithmetic overflows".
That is why server limits on header size, header count, body size and read timeouts are security settings, not just tuning.

pages.title: HTTP 204 Is the Best DELETE Response - by Bruno Pedro
passages: # [The API Changelog](/)
# HTTP 204 Is the Best DELETE Response
### Sometimes, an empty response is the best response.
"The best response for an HTTP DELETE operation is not an HTTP 200 status code with whatever response body you come up with." That's how I started a post I published on social media a few days ago.
What I thought was that the post would get a few likes and, at best, a couple of comments.
What I didn't anticipate was that the post would grow to a couple of hundred reactions (likes included) and almost one hundred comments.
One hundred comments from dozens of people sharing their opinions about the best response for an HTTP DELETE operation.
Did they all agree with me?
Keep reading to find out.
The first few comments I received were all positive.
Everyone seemed to agree that the best response for an HTTP DELETE would be a 204 code with an empty body.
Some of those early comments even highlighted the advantages a 204 has over other responses.
Other comments opened threads between participants about other HTTP methods and their responses.
Overall, there was a multitude of opinions being shared as comments on that post of mine.
One comment that caught my attention asked why I advocated for an empty body.
Its author couldn't understand why I didn't favor a response that included information about the status of the delete operation.
Or, why I didn't bother to include the number of successfully deleted items in the response.
My opinion is simple.
The status of the delete operation is successful if the response is empty and the HTTP status code is 204.
Otherwise, the response will include an HTTP error, and its body will include the corresponding details.
About the number of deleted items, I see the HTTP DELETE as an operation that affects one single item, not many.
Therefore, there's no need to think about responding with information about the number of deleted items.
A few other comments insisted on responding with an HTTP 200 with a body that includes information about the deleted item.
The authors of those comments stated that some consumers could see value in using information about the deleted item after the fact.
The way I see it, if consumers really need the information about the deleted item, they can obtain it by making an HTTP GET request to read the item before deleting it.
They could even show the information to an end user and ask for confirmation before attempting a delete operation.
Then, receiving an HTTP 204 is a sign that the delete operation was successful, and there's no need to receive any other information.
And, I'm not the only one who thinks that way.
Some of the people who agreed with my opinion took their time to share why an HTTP 204 is the best option.
Some comments mentioned MDN, in particular their explanation of the [HTTP 204 status code](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/204).

According to MDN, and generally speaking, a 204 "indicates that a request has succeeded, but the client doesn't need to navigate away from its current page." MDN refers to "current page" in the context of frontend development.
If you're dealing with a backend implementation it means that the client doesn't need to load more information.

MDN goes further and explains that, in response to an HTTP DELETE, it means that the "action was successful, and no further information needs to be supplied." I really like the way MDN explains that the detail is in the fact that API consumers don't need further information.
On their [HTTP DELETE documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/DELETE), they reiterate that.
There, they recommend a 204 as the first response to a DELETE operation.
Another source of wisdom that other people referred to is RFC 9110 ("HTTP Semantics") from June 2022.
This document obsoletes RFC 7231, which was the one generally referred to when discussing HTTP semantics.
So, looking at the [RFC 9110 section 9.3.5 about the DELETE method](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-delete), I can immediately notice the types of responses it recommends.
Here, the 204 response isn't the first suggestion but it's still recommended before an HTTP 200 response.
To summarize, they first recommend responding with a 202 if the action will "likely succeed" but hasn't yet been enacted.

Then they recommend a 204 if the action has been enacted and "no further information is to be supplied." Finally, they recommend the 200 only if you need to respond with "a representation describing the status." Again, here, there's a clear preference for not sharing further information after a successful DELETE operation.
So, why do I think that not returning any information is the best approach?
One reason has to do with the nature of the information you'd return after a successful DELETE.
Would you return an ID of the deleted resource, a timestamp of the operation, or something else?
My perspective is that the API consumer already knows the ID of the deleted resource because it's part of the request URI.
And, the timestamp is returned on the `Date` response header.
So, there's no need to add that same information to the response body.
The only situation where I'd see value in a response body is when you're attempting to delete multiple resources at once.
Then, it could be interesting to receive a list of the IDs of the deleted resources.
To conclude, I'm not saying that an HTTP 204 with an empty body is the only response to a DELETE operation.
What I'm saying is that it's the best one.
In any case, I found that having this debate was positive as I learned a lot from the comments and opened up to new ideas.

Oh, and before I forget, here's the [original LinkedIn post](https://web.archive.org/web/20250604104302/https://www.linkedin.com/posts/bpedro_the-best-response-for-an-http-delete-operation-activity-7333127712040968192-elTa?rcm=ACoAAAANpdkBRvW5OuzgJ3nkzQ4JUKFbgxwXpYU) where all the discussion happened, kindly preserved by the Wayback Machine.

# Using additional HTTP verbs when your client is limited
There are some cases where apps can't make HTTP requests with verbs other than GET or POST.
For example, some proxies, firewalls, etc. might be configured by their operators to block certain HTTP verbs, or certain app environments might not support other verbs.
For these cases, the OneDrive API provides an alternative way of specifying an HTTP verb when necessary.
You can tunnel any HTTP request through a POST by making a POST request and adding the `X-HTTP-Method-Override` header set to the method you want to invoke.
This signals the server to process the request not as a POST, but as whatever verb was specified as the value of that header.
This header is only valid for POST requests.
It will be ignored for other HTTP methods.
For example, if the DELETE verb is blocked by a firewall, your application can tunnel the verb to the API to ensure that your app can still delete a file.
POST /drive/items/{item-id} HTTP/1.1 Host: api.onedrive.com X-HTTP-Method-Override: DELETE
This request will delete the resource identified.
The response from the service will match the response that would have been returned if the HTTP method had DELETE.
